impacts.caseName: Dental Monitoring SAS v. Align Technology, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board's Penumbra framework—holding that Dynamic Drinkware's written description analysis does not apply to prior art determinations under AIA § 102(d)(2)—is correct, and what standard governs whether a reference patent receives the filing date of an earlier provisional application for prior art purposes under the AIA.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's finding that claims of a dental imaging patent were obvious, questioning the Board's approach to determining when a reference patent qualifies for an earlier provisional application filing date as prior art under AIA § 102(d)(2). The court remanded for reconsideration of whether the prior art reference was entitled to its provisional filing date. This decision has significant implications for how provisional application dates are used to establish prior art in IPR proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from heightened scrutiny of whether reference patents are entitled to earlier provisional filing dates, potentially narrowing the pool of prior art available to challengers in IPR proceedings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies challenging patents in IPR proceedings may find it more difficult to rely on reference patents' provisional filing dates as prior art, increasing the cost and complexity of invalidity challenges.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 applies differently to method claims (e.g., methods of treating headache with anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies) than to composition claims, and whether broad functional method claims are adequately enabled when any member of the claimed genus would be effective.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a panel decision upholding Teva's broad method claims for treating headaches with anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies against Eli Lilly's enablement challenge. Judge Dyk dissented, arguing the panel decision creates confusion about enablement standards for method claims and sustains overly broad claims contrary to Supreme Court precedent. This decision is highly significant for pharmaceutical and biotech patent strategy.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with broad method-of-treatment claims benefit from a more permissive enablement standard, allowing broader patent protection for biologic drugs and therapeutic methods.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar companies face broader blocking patents on therapeutic methods, potentially delaying market entry and increasing litigation risk when challenging enablement of broad biologic drug patents.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding Versata's trade secret damages expert and in its judgment on trade secret misappropriation damages and breach of contract damages arising from Ford's development of competing software while licensing Versata's technology.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court also reversed the breach of contract damages ruling and reinstated the jury award, while affirming Ford's liability for trade secret misappropriation. This case provides important guidance on permissible damages methodologies in trade secret misappropriation cases involving software licensing relationships.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software licensors and trade secret holders benefit from expanded damages theories being available at trial, and the reinstatement of the jury's breach of contract award strengthens enforcement of technology licensing agreements.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop competing products while licensing third-party technology face significant trade secret misappropriation exposure, with broader damages models potentially available to plaintiffs on retrial.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' in the licensed patents such that the licensee could sue for infringement without joining the patent owner, and whether the licensee's shift to an enforcement-only business model triggered an automatic termination clause.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that the exclusive license agreement between Texas A&M and TexasLDPC conveyed all substantial rights in the asserted patents, entitling TexasLDPC to sue without joining A&M. The court also held that TexasLDPC's shift to patent enforcement did not constitute cessation of business operations triggering automatic termination. This decision clarifies when exclusive licensees have standing to enforce patents independently.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees and patent assertion entities benefit from clearer standards confirming their ability to enforce patents without joining university or corporate patent owners, facilitating patent monetization structures.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a potential defense based on challenging the standing of exclusive licensees, and the decision may encourage more patent enforcement by licensing entities separated from original patent owners.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems satisfy the patent eligibility requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court's damages award and infringement findings were proper.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the eligibility determination for certain patent claims related to non-uniform constellation technology used in digital communications while affirming eligibility for other claims, affirming the infringement and damages findings. The court remanded for further proceedings on the vacated claims. This decision provides important guidance on the application of Alice/Mayo patent eligibility analysis to communications technology patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies holding patents on digital communication improvements benefit from the affirmance of eligibility for certain claims and the upholding of infringement and damages findings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Electronics manufacturers and standards implementers face continued patent infringement liability for standards-essential technology, and the partial vacatur on eligibility creates ongoing uncertainty about the scope of patent-eligible subject matter in communications technology.

impacts.caseName: Range of Motion Products, LLC v. Armaid Company Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit's design patent infringement framework under Egyptian Goddess improperly focuses on differences rather than overall similarity, and whether claim construction involving functionality determinations in design patents raises factual questions for the jury.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing in a design patent case, with a divided court debating whether the Egyptian Goddess framework improperly emphasizes differences between designs rather than overall similarity when assessing infringement. The concurrence defended the existing framework, while the dissent (joined by four judges) argued the court's approach has shifted the infringement inquiry away from the Supreme Court's Gorham standard and improperly resolves factual questions at summary judgment.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the continued application of a framework that permits summary judgment of non-infringement based on visual differences between patented and accused designs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Design patent holders face a heightened risk of losing infringement cases at summary judgment, as the existing framework may overemphasize differences between designs rather than requiring a holistic assessment of overall similarity by a jury.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims of a communications apparatus patent are invalid for lack of enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a), even though the district court's indefiniteness ruling was erroneous.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's indefiniteness finding but affirmed the final judgment of invalidity on alternative enablement grounds raised by Samsung. The court held that while the patent claims were definite, they were not enabled because the specification did not teach a person of ordinary skill how to practice the full scope of the claims. This decision demonstrates the Federal Circuit's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds, providing multiple avenues for challenging patent validity.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face the risk that even if they prevail on one invalidity ground, courts may still invalidate their patents on alternative theories raised by defendants.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has subject-matter jurisdiction over a dispute concerning the interpretation of a patent settlement agreement's contingent payment clause tied to the outcome of an ex parte reexamination, or whether the dispute is purely a state law contract interpretation matter.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked jurisdiction over a dispute about whether T-Mobile owed a contingent payment under a patent settlement agreement conditioned on asserted claims 'surviving' an ex parte reexamination. The court found the dispute was fundamentally a state law contract interpretation question that did not necessarily depend on resolving a substantial patent law question, and transferred the case to the Fifth Circuit. This decision clarifies jurisdictional boundaries for patent-related settlement disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Parties to patent settlement agreements benefit from clarity that contract disputes over settlement terms will be resolved by regional circuits applying state contract law, potentially providing more predictable interpretation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Parties may face strategic disadvantage or increased costs when patent settlement disputes are routed to regional circuits less experienced in patent-related contexts, and the decision may complicate forum planning for patent settlement agreements.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court provided sufficient reasoning in denying a defendant's motion for Rule 11 sanctions and attorneys' fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 where the plaintiff pursued patent infringement claims after the PTO rejected related patent claims under § 101 post-Alice.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's denial of sanctions and attorneys' fees, finding the court's order provided insufficient detail for meaningful appellate review. The case involved a plaintiff that continued to assert a patent after the PTO had rejected claims in related applications under § 101 following Alice, and after a related patent was invalidated under § 101 in another district court action. This decision signals closer scrutiny of continued patent assertion after adverse § 101 rulings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from increased judicial scrutiny of fee-shifting motions and stronger deterrence against continuation of patent suits where related claims have been rejected or invalidated under § 101.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders and their counsel face heightened risk of sanctions and fee awards for pursuing infringement claims after adverse § 101 rulings in related proceedings, requiring more careful pre-suit analysis of patent eligibility.

impacts.caseName: Exelixis, Inc. v. MSN Laboratories Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether pharmaceutical patents claiming crystalline forms of cabozantinib (L)-malate salts satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a) when the specification discloses the salt and crystalline forms but the claims encompass forms that were not individually characterized.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding that Exelixis's pharmaceutical patents covering crystalline cabozantinib malate salts had adequate written description, rejecting MSN's invalidity challenge. This decision is significant for pharmaceutical patent strategy as it upholds broad crystalline form claims for a blockbuster cancer drug (Cabometyx), reinforcing protection against generic entry until 2030.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical innovators benefit from the affirmance of written description adequacy for crystalline polymorph patents, supporting broader patent protection strategies for drug formulations and potentially extending market exclusivity.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies face stronger barriers to market entry when branded drug manufacturers hold validated crystalline form patents, potentially delaying the availability of lower-cost generic alternatives.

impacts.caseName: Archroma U.S., Inc. v. Department of Commerce
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce's regulation imposing a 15-day deadline for domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in sunset reviews of antidumping duty orders conflicts with the governing statute, which is silent on filing deadlines.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade's invalidation of Commerce's regulation requiring domestic interested parties to file within 15 days of a sunset review initiation notice. The court held that the statute's silence on deadlines did not preclude Commerce from imposing one through rulemaking, and that the 15-day deadline was a permissible exercise of the agency's delegated authority. This decision preserves Commerce's procedural framework for antidumping sunset reviews that protect domestic industries from dumped imports.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic manufacturers benefit from the reinstatement of Commerce's procedural framework for antidumping sunset reviews, preserving the agency's ability to efficiently manage trade remedy proceedings that protect against unfair foreign competition.
impacts.negativeImplications: Importers and foreign producers face continued strict procedural requirements in sunset reviews, with the 15-day participation deadline potentially disadvantaging parties who miss the narrow filing window.
